title: Modules, paths and privacy
summary: Group related code into modules, make items public with pub, name them with absolute and relative paths, reach the parent with super, and see how privacy works for struct fields and enum variants.

sections: TRPL 7.2 Defining Modules to Control Scope and Privacy
TRPL 7.3 Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree
TRPL 7.3 Exposing Paths with the pub Keyword
TRPL 7.3 Starting Relative Paths with super
TRPL 7.3 Making Structs and Enums Public
PR ch8 Making struct Fields pub

blocks.md:
A **module** is a named container for items: functions, structs, enums, constants and other modules. Modules do two jobs. They **organize** code into groups that a reader can navigate, and they control **privacy**: whether code outside the module may use an item.

*The Rust Programming Language* uses a restaurant as its example. The **front of house** is where customers are: hosts seat them, servers take orders and payment. The **back of house** is the kitchen, which customers never see. A library for running a restaurant mirrors that split:

blocks.explain: `mod name { ... }` defines a module inline. Modules nest. The crate root is an implicit module named `crate`, so this file forms a tree.

blocks.title: The module tree
blocks.code:
crate
 └── front_of_house
     ├── hosting
     │   ├── add_to_waitlist
     │   └── seat_at_table
     └── serving
         ├── take_order
         ├── serve_order
         └── take_payment
blocks.explain: It looks like a file-system tree, and you navigate it like one, with paths.

blocks.title: Paths
blocks.md:
To use an item you name it with a **path**, with `::` between the parts:

- An **absolute path** starts at the crate root with `crate`: `crate::front_of_house::hosting::add_to_waitlist()`.
- A **relative path** starts from the current module, with a module name, `self` (this module) or `super` (the parent module).

Which to use? Ask whether the calling code is more likely to move together with the item or separately. Absolute paths survive moving the caller; relative paths survive moving both together. Absolute paths are the more common default.

blocks.title: Private by default
blocks.md: Every item is **private** to its parent module unless marked `pub`. Code in a module can see everything in its own module and in its **ancestors**, but not inside its children. In the restaurant: the kitchen can see the dining room, but customers cannot see the kitchen. Privacy lets a module change its internals freely, as long as its public items keep working.

blocks.title: super
blocks.md: `super::` starts a path in the parent module, like `..` in a file system. It is handy for an item that is closely tied to its parent and likely to move with it:

blocks.title: Public structs and enums
blocks.md:
For a **struct**, `pub` makes the type public, but **each field stays private** unless marked `pub` too. That is how a type protects its rules: if a field is private, outside code cannot build the struct with `Struct { ... }` at all, so the module must offer a constructor.

For an **enum**, `pub` makes **all its variants public**. An enum whose variants you cannot see would be useless.

blocks.explain: Uncomment the `seasonal_fruit` line and the compiler reports `error[E0616]: field `seasonal_fruit` of struct `Breakfast` is private`. Because one field is private, `main` could not even write `Breakfast { toast: ..., seasonal_fruit: ... }`; it must call `summer`.

blocks.title: Finer-grained visibility
blocks.md: Besides `pub` there are `pub(crate)` (visible anywhere in this crate, but not to other crates) and `pub(super)` (visible to the parent module). `pub(crate)` is common for helpers that several modules share but that are not part of the library's public API.

blocks.title: Open just enough
blocks.md: `main` wants to create a temperature reading with `sensors::Reading::new` and print it, but almost everything is private. Add the **minimum** `pub` keywords to make it compile: the `celsius` field must stay private (there is a getter), and `calibrate` must stay private too.
hints: Read the errors one at a time: each one names the private item.
Four `pub`s: the struct, the `id` field, and the `new` and `celsius` methods. `calibrate` is called from inside the module, so it can stay private.

blocks.title: A library with a public face
blocks.goal: Organize code into nested modules with the right visibility, so the public API is small and the rules are enforced inside.
blocks.behavior:
In `src/lib.rs`, create:
- `pub mod catalog` with `pub struct Item { pub title: String, copies: u32 }` and methods `pub fn new(title: &str, copies: u32) -> Item`, `pub fn copies(&self) -> u32`, and `pub(crate) fn take(&mut self) -> bool` (removes one copy if there is one).
- `pub mod loans` with `pub fn borrow(item: &mut crate::catalog::Item) -> Result<(), String>`: calls `take`; returns `Err(format!("no copies of {}", title))` when none are left.
- At the crate root, `pub fn stock_report(items: &[catalog::Item]) -> String`: one line per item, `"<title>: <copies>"`, joined with `\n`.
The tests use `crate::catalog::Item::new`, `crate::loans::borrow` and `crate::stock_report`. `copies` must stay private.

examples.output: Ok(()), then Err("no copies of Dune")

hints: `take` is `pub(crate)` so `loans` can call it but users of the library cannot.
Inside `loans`, refer to the item type as `crate::catalog::Item` or `super::catalog::Item`.
`stock_report`: build a `Vec<String>` of lines with `format!` and `join("\n")` it, or push onto a `String` and add `\n` between lines.
blocks.solution_explain: Outside the crate, the only way to change `copies` is `loans::borrow`, which checks the rule. `take` is `pub(crate)`: visible to `loans` but not part of the public API. The `use` at the top of `loans` is next lesson's topic; writing the full path `crate::catalog::Item` works just as well.

questions.q: Without any `pub`, who can call a function inside `mod kitchen`?
options: Only code in `kitchen` and its child modules
questions.explanation: Private items are visible in their own module and its descendants.

questions.q: `pub struct User { name: String }` is in a module. Can code outside write `User { name: s }`?
questions.explanation: Fields are private unless marked `pub` themselves, and a struct literal needs every field.

questions.q: Marking an enum `pub` makes all of its variants public.
questions.explanation: Unlike struct fields, enum variants share the enum's visibility.

points: `mod name { ... }` groups items; modules form a tree rooted at `crate`.
Paths name items: absolute from `crate::`, relative from the current module, `self` or `super`.
Everything is private by default; children can see their ancestors, not the other way round.
`pub` must be added at every step of the path outside code uses.
Struct fields are private unless marked `pub`; enum variants are public with the enum.

terms.def: A named container of items that organizes code and controls privacy.
A name for an item, with parts separated by ::, like crate::front_of_house::hosting.
Items are private to their parent module unless marked pub; private items are hidden from outside code.
A path start that refers to the parent module.
Visibility that makes an item usable anywhere in the same crate, but not by other crates.
